summary: Discovery focused on per-token economics, tradeoffs between hosted/dedicated/private, batching and KV caching levers, and a constrained monthly budget. Customer expressed strong SLA and encryption/KMS requirements for regulated telemetry. Agreed next steps: pricing workbook, benchmark artifacts, and pilot acceptance criteria.
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
transcript:
00:00 Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone thanks for making time. Quick intro, I'm Alex, AE on this. Today we'll walk pricing pathways, pilot scope, SLA needs. Priya is on to talk performance.
00:18 Jordan (Greenspire CTO): Hi all. Quick context—we're building a near real-time inference stream for grid alerts, mostly short prompts ~60 tokens but some longer histories up to 1k. Our monthly budget target is around $18k to start for pilot.
00:33 Maya (Head of ML): And quality matters; can't have hallucinations in actionable alerts.
00:39 Priya (Redwood SE): Great, two big buckets: unit economics and deployment mode. For unit econ, hosted per-token looks simple: you pay per input+output token, and we optimize with batching and prefix KV caching to lower effective tokens. Dedicated gives lower unit cost at scale but requires commit. Private gives control but higher ops and infra cost.
00:58 Alex: Quick q to Maya and Jordan — is the $18k a hard ceiling, or flexible if latency requires more?
01:05 Jordan: It's a pretty hard runway for Q3 pilot. We could flex a bit if the business case is clear.
01:12 Sam (SRE): Important: our SRE team requires 99.9% availability and p99 tail latency < 250ms for short prompts. If we can't hit that we need routing/fallbacks.
01:24 Priya: OK that's helpful. For p99 <250ms on short prompts, many customers choose Dedicated or Redwood-hosted with reserved capacity in region. Private on-prem can meet it but adds network hops and ops variability.
01:37 Maya: What are the main levers to push down cost? Batching obviously but that increases latency. KV cache sounds interesting — how often does it save tokens?
01:47 Priya: So KV/prefix cache helps when you have repeated context — you only pay decoding tokens for new tokens, and KV cache eliminates recomputing the earlier tokens. In practice with conversational history patterns we've seen 25-60% token savings depending on overlap. It depends on repeat rates.
02:04 Jordan: Our typical flow has a 150-token recent context with mostly repeated system instructions and 2–3 previous user messages. Sounds promising.
02:12 Alex: Also quantization options reduce infer compute cost on Dedicated/Private. On hosted we surface quantized model variants that lower per-token cost but may affect quality slightly.
02:22 Maya: Are quantized variants available for our models or do we need custom?
02:26 Priya: We have a catalog of Redwood-verified quantized variants; for highly-sensitive prompts we recommend running evals before switching in production. We'll include recommended quant profiles in the workbook.
02:36 Jordan: Security note — we need KMS integration (customer-managed keys), audit logs, and SOC2 Type II. Can hosted meet that?
02:44 Alex: Hosted can integrate with customer KMS and we provide audit logs and SOC2. For the strictest controls some customers move to Private to keep keys fully within their VPC/HSM. We'll share our security pack PDF link.
02:58 Ellen (Procurement): On procurement timeline: if pilot pricing looks good we can sign a month-to-month pilot contract and plan enterprise terms later. Send draft SOW and pricing tables.
03:08 Priya: I want to unpack the latency vs batching tradeoff with a quick example — if you do micro-batching windows of 50ms you'll increase throughput and lower per-token cost but p99 may spike; larger batch windows reduce cost more. Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching with latency SLOs so you can tune thresholds.
03:30 Sam: Do you have numbers? Like per-token cost delta between single-request low-latency path and 100ms batch?
03:36 Priya: Rough ballpark: for an Llama-class 13B-ish variant, single-request low-latency might be $0.0009 per token, 50ms batching could drop to $0.0006, and 100ms batching to $0.00045. These are illustrative; we'll put exact scenarios in the workbook.
03:53 Maya: Hmm that matters. Our alerts are time-sensitive — 250ms p99 is tight. We need to know which combo keeps p99 under 250ms while staying under budget.
04:03 Alex: That's exactly the pilot decision — test 1: hosted reserved capacity with small batch windows; test 2: Dedicated small commit with aggressive batching; test 3: Private concierge deployment for worst-case latency. We'll map costs.
04:18 Jordan: For Dedicated, what's commit size typical?
04:20 Priya: Commits vary. Many customers start with a monthly GPU-equivalent commit (e.g., 4k-8k GPU-hours depending on model). Dedicated gives lower per-token rate once amortized. We'll include example TCOs for 3, 6, 12 month commits.
04:33 Alex: Quick aside — competitors like MacroModel pitch cheaper per-token but don't provide KV cache or rollouts which help production stability.
04:42 Jordan: Noted. Also need to know about automatic fallback — if dedicated capacity hits limit can requests seamlessly fall back to hosted?
04:50 Priya: Yes, smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants in hosted or other pools. You can set cost-priority or latency-priority routing policies.
05:01 Sam: Network question for Private: can we bring our own HSM for keys?
05:05 Alex: Yes, customer-managed HSM/KMS is an option for Private and some Dedicated architectures. We'll document the network topology and firewall rules needed.
05:15 Maya: About evaluation — we want to run a 2-week pilot with a 100k requests/day profile peaking at 350 qps. Is that realistic?
05:24 Priya: 350 qps sustained is non-trivial but doable with Dedicated. For hosted we'd recommend reserved concurrency in region and maybe a small burst pool. We'll model those and show required commit or target request-limits.
05:35 Jordan: OK. On success criteria — low false positive rate below 2% and p99 <250ms for short prompts. If we hit those and stay under $18k that's a win.
05:45 Alex: Great — clear acceptance criteria. I'll capture that in the SOW.
05:49 Speaker 1 (auto): [inaudible] ...
06:02 Priya: A couple more nuances — caching helps more when you have repeated prefix templates. If your templates are highly variable you'll see less benefit. Also, tokenization matters: some domain-specific wording increases token count.
06:18 Maya: We have lots of domain terms and meter readings, likely more tokens per message. We'll send sample traces.
06:24 Alex: Please send anonymized logs and sample payloads; that will let us run quick tokenization and estimate real token counts and cost.
06:33 Jordan: Security again — SSO and RBAC. We use Okta. Need SAML and role mapping.
06:39 Alex: We support SAML/Okta and fine-grained RBAC in Console for model access and routes. We'll add docs.
06:46 Ellen: Procurement follow-up — do you require upfront payment?
06:50 Alex: For pilot usually month-to-month invoice; for Dedicated commits we typically require upfront or net-30 depending on contract. We'll surface options in the pricing workbook.
07:02 Priya: Let me give an example math run — assume average 220 tokens per request including history, 100k requests/day gives ~22M tokens/day, at $0.0006/token that's $13.2k/day which is obviously too high so you'd leverage caching and batch to reduce that. Real pilot numbers will be far lower when caching reduces decode tokens by 50% and batching lowers per-token compute.
07:28 Maya: That example is concerning — good thing we will run actual tokenization.
07:34 Priya: Right. We'll run a small synthetic benchmark with your sample traces and show modeled monthly cost under different setups.
07:41 Jordan: Also curious about metrics and observability — can the Console show token-level breakdown per route?
07:46 Carlos (Redwood SE): Yes, Console has per-route token/cost, latency histograms, and tracing hooks you can ship to your APM. You can set alerts on token spikes.
07:55 Sam: Will we get per-request IDs for correlation?
07:58 Carlos: Yes, request IDs and trace headers.
08:02 Maya: About model variants — what if we want an Llama-2.2 style open model quantized?
08:07 Priya: We can host vetted open models and provide quantized variants. We also support private model imports on Dedicated/Private if you want to bring custom weights.
08:16 Jordan: If we bring our own model, what's the impact on cost and performance?
08:20 Priya: That depends on the model size and kernel compatibility. Sometimes custom models are more efficient; other times they need special optimization passes. We'll run a quick perf test during pilot.
08:30 Alex: Let's talk timeline: aim to start pilot in early August, 2-week run in August 10–24, with readiness milestones: sample traces by 7/22, pilot SOW signed by 7/28, and security review by 7/30.
08:45 Ellen: That timeline seems doable.
08:49 Jordan: One more question — preemptible GPUs to lower cost? We have concerns about interruption.
08:54 Priya: Preemptible can cut infra cost but increases interruption risk and cold-starts. For production with tight p99 we avoid preemptible for critical pools; they can be used for background batch jobs.
09:05 Maya: Good to know.
09:09 Alex: Alright let's recap next steps and owners. Alex will send pricing workbook and security pack; Priya will share benchmark script and quant profiles; Jordan/Maya will send sample traces and SLA definitions; Ellen will confirm procurement windows.
09:25 Jordan: Thanks everyone. Looking forward to the workbook.
09:28 Alex: Thanks, we'll follow up.
09:31 [meeting ends]
